Welcome to Women's Media Center Live. I'm Robin Morgan. Today we're going to explore the United States House of Representatives, the People's House. Fortunately, it's not anywhere near as riddled with unspoken rules and unwritten traditions as is the Senate, and in general it tends to be livelier, which can be a good thing at times and maybe not so much at other times. Besides, it currently has Nancy Pelosi in her second term as the first woman speaker of the House. My special guest today is Congresswoman Val Demings, Democrat of Florida and former house manager for the first impeachment trial of Donald Trump. She's a former police chief and she's tough and tender and terrific all at the same time. And of course, there's surrealism corner and fighting words, but before we get into any of that, we need to go inside the headlines. The United States House of Representatives and the United States Senate are modeled respectively on the British House of Commons and House of Lords, the latter having longer terms, being originally selected not by popular vote, but by each state legislature, and assumed to be further removed from the popular politics of the so-called rabble, thus better insulated to consider great matters of the nation. The US Senate was designed to represent the states, that each state would stand in a relationship of equality with the others. It was an expression of federalism. The US House of Representatives was designed to represent the nation. It was the expression of democracy, representing the people. The House of Representatives is the only branch of government directly elected by American voters since its formation in 1789. In the very first Congress, there were only 65 representatives the number grew over time as new states joined the country and the population grew. But in 1911, Congress decided the House was getting too big. So they passed a law limiting the number of representatives to 435. The number from each state is determined by the population of the state. The more people who live in the state, the more representatives the state has. Except that this does not account for gerrymandering, about which more in a minute. Every state has at least one representative, no matter how small it is. Proportional representation, really the heart of the American Revolution, is where the census becomes vitally important. According to some scholars and historians, since the house's number 435 was developed only in the reapportionment act of 1924, there's no reason there can't be more representatives per state. All Congress would need to do, as it did in 1924, is decide on a good number and divide up the congressional districts accordingly. So, as an aside, one change people really might consider when discussing structural change in D.C. would be to enlarge the house, giving the more populous states more power. Still, even as is, direct biennial elections and the size of the membership, currently 435 voting representatives, have made the House receptive to a continual influx of new ideas and priorities that contribute to its long-standing reputation as the People's House. Benjamin Franklin, Pennsylvania delegate to the Constitutional Convention, summed up the desired balance. Quote, If a proportional representation takes place, the small states contend that their liberties will be in danger. If an equality of votes is to be put in its place, the large states say their money will be in danger. When a broad table is to be made and the edges of planks don't fit, the artist takes a little from both and makes a good joint." So did the great compromise create a bicameral legislature, enabling the convention which was teetering on the brink of dissolution to continue. This, in turn, relied on the census, which, however, proved highly controversial. Southern delegates argued that their slaves counted in the population yielding them more representatives, although enslaved persons couldn't vote. Northern delegates countered that slaves were property and should not be counted at all. The result was the notorious three-fifths compromise, where each enslaved person was counted as three-fifths of a free person. The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified after the Civil War, began to remedy this infamous compromise by ordering the census to fully count every male individual, regardless of skin color. All female citizens had to wait for the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920. While the number of House members for each state is determined according to a statistical formula in federal law, each state is responsible for designing the shape of its district so long as it accords with various provisions of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which seeks to protect racial minorities voting and representation rights, or used to, but it was gutted recently by the Supreme Court, giving gerrymandering free rein. The Speaker of the House political and parliamentary leader of that body is second in line to becoming President of the United States after the Vice President. The speaker's position has evolved considerably over time, originating in the British House of Commons during the 14th century when the speaker had allegiances to the legislative body as well as to the sovereign. In the 18th century, speakers served as party leaders and ministers of government. The American speakership has grown from being held by regional or party leaders into a powerful post with the authority to appoint members to house standing committees and the authority to control the flow of legislation to the floor. And then in the 1970s, after reforms limiting committee power, the authority of house speakers re-emerged as the coordination and timing of legislation gained greater importance. The framers initially set 21, the voting age, as the minimum age to serve in the House. During the Federal Constitutional Convention, though, George Mason of Virginia moved to make the age 25, saying there should be a period between being free to manage one's own affairs and managing those of a great nation, the amendment passed. But generally, the Constitution placed few hurdles for an ordinary citizen becoming a member of the House, among them being a U.S. citizen for at least seven years, living in the same state, though not necessarily the same district represented, and taking an oath to support the Constitution. James Madison wrote, quote, under these reasonable limitations, the door of this part of the federal government is open to merit of every description, whether native or adoptive, whether young or old and without regard to poverty or wealth or to any particular profession of religious faith. Among the special duties mandated for the House of Representatives are that the House has the power to name the President in case of a tie in the Electoral College. While members of Congress are expressly forbidden from being electors, The Constitution requires the House and Senate to count the Electoral College's ballots, and in the event of a tie, select the President and Vice President. This was the duty they were performing on January 6th when the Capitol was besieged. The Constitution gives the House the sole power to impeach an official, and it makes the Senate the sole court for impeachment trials. The power of impeachment is limited to removal from office, but also provides a means by which a removed officer may be disqualified from holding future office. Fines and potential jail time for crimes committed in office are left to the courts. Congress has the power to provide for the common defense and general welfare of the United States, that is, to declare war, to make rules conquering captures on land and water, to raise and support armies, Provide and maintain a navy, provide for calling forth the militia to execute the laws of the Union, suppress insurrections, and repel invasions, et cetera. The framers of the Constitution denied the president authority to go to war unilaterally. For most of U.S. history, the Constitution's checks and balances worked, and more often than not, presidents sought the consent of Congress on war matters. Nevertheless, over time, the executive branch began to assume more and more power in declaring hostilities, fulfilling Madison's dire prediction to Jefferson that, quote, the executive is a branch of power most interested in war and most prone to it. Period, close quote. This power remains a matter of contention and debate since the President is also named Commander-in-Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States and of the militia of the several states when called into the actual service of the United States. The Constitution also mandates that all bills for raising revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives, although the Senate may propose or concur with amendments as on other bills, then that no money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in consequence of appropriations made by law. Thus, the House is invested with the power of the purse. Following the maxim that since the house was more immediately representative of the people, the people were to hold the purse strings. The House of Representatives may determine the rules of its proceedings, punish its members for disorderly behavior, and with the concurrence of two-thirds of members expel a member. In practice, the most severe type of punishment is expulsion, requiring that two-thirds majority vote. censure and reprimand are imposed by a simple majority vote of the full house. Expulsion has traditionally been reserved for only the most reprehensible conduct or crimes, such as treasonable acts. Indeed, the first three individuals expelled from the house had taken up arms for the rebel confederacy during the Civil War. The House, along with the Senate, has vested in themselves in investigative powers, and the Supreme Court has determined that the framers intended for Congress to seek out information when crafting or reviewing legislation. Such investigations include the powerful tools of subpoena power and of being held in contempt of Congress. In the Federalist Number 52, James Madison of Virginia, who would become the first former House member to later serve as president, wrote, quote, as it is essential to liberty that the government in general should have a common interest with the people. So it is particularly essential that the branch of it under consideration should have an immediate dependence on and an intimate sympathy with the people." Hence, the biennial elections, the shorter terms, and the overall designation as the people's house. Technology has tried to keep pace with that designation. In 1844, Samuel Moore sent the first official telegraph from the capital. In 1947, the first live television broadcast from the house chamber took place. during the 80th Congress. In 1973, the first electronic vote was lodged in the House of Representatives, and in March 1979, the House inaugurated live, televised, gavel to gavel debate on the House floor. The American Revolution was, in part, a contest about the very definition of representation. In England, the House of Commons represented every British subject, regardless of whether the subject could actually vote for its membership. In this sense, most people living in areas under British rule, including North America, were only virtually represented in Parliament. American colonists accustomed to controlling their local affairs in directly elected colonial legislatures, resented British policies imposed on them, such as London imposing taxes without the benefit of a voice in Parliament. Thus they rallied behind the motto, no taxation without representation. Representation was closely linked to taxation. Before federal income taxes or tariffs, the states contributed to the national government with local taxes, often flat poll taxes on each citizen. Since constitutional framers had to provide for funding the new government, they debated the proper relationship between representation and taxation. Several delegates argued that geographic size or usable farmland were better measures of state wealth than population. Delegates, however, settled on proportional contributions based on population and, by extension, the number of members in the House of Representatives. Large states with more human capital should contribute more revenue to the national government and also have more seats in the legislature as a result. This fulfilled the promise of the American Revolution, taxation with representation. Then there are term lengths. English parliamentary elections and meetings of the House of Commons varied between three and seven-year terms, but elections and meetings were set by the members themselves and often were tied to the demands of the King. American Convention delegates argued heatedly about the terms of service for House members, and the founders employed their experiences with the House of Commons and with state legislatures when designing the new federal government. Two innovations to further democratic accountability separated the American and British experiences. The first was fixed terms of office. Unlike in parliamentary systems, American political parties could not call advantageous elections whenever political leaders thought they'd be most likely to win. Instead, elections would be held according to a given length of time. The second innovation was regular elections. One and three year terms of service were initially proposed. Proponents of the one-year term used their state legislatures as an example, while proponents of the three-year term followed the British example. Framers who favored longer terms argued that it would help the Senate track the democratic impulses of the House. Remember that the French Revolution had just occurred with all its bloody excesses, and these men were highly alarmed at the thought of mob rule, as our own recent experience with populist demigogary and mob insurrection demonstrate. The convention settled on two-year terms for the House as a compromise between the one and three-year factions. Frequent elections in the House also helped to justify the longer terms of Senators, particularly for Federalists, who were concerned about popular opinion swaying public policy and who faced attacks for creating a so-called aristocratic chamber in Congress, the Senate, to represent state interests.
